description: Learn Python's data types, variables, constants and how to write readable code.
content_html:
Why Data Types Matter

Every value stored in a Python program has a data type. Choosing the right type is not optional — it determines what you can do with the data. You cannot multiply two strings together arithmetically. You cannot store the word “open” as a Boolean. Getting the type wrong causes errors that are often tricky to diagnose. Python works with five primitive data types you must know, plus structured types for grouping data together.

Key Fact

The five primitive data types are: integer (whole number, e.g. 7 or -3), real (decimal number, e.g. 3.14 — Python calls this float), Boolean (True or False), char (a single character, e.g. 'A'), and string (a sequence of characters, e.g. "hello"). In your exam, use the term real rather than float in written answers.

The Primitive Data Types in Python

An integer stores a whole number. Examples include a player’s score, the number of students in a class, or a person’s age. In Python, you write: age = 16.

A real stores values with a fractional part. Examples include a temperature reading (36.7), a price (12.99), or a percentage (78.5). In Python: temperature = 36.7.

A Boolean holds only one of two values: True or False. Note the capital first letter — Python is case-sensitive. Examples: whether a user is logged in, whether a door sensor is triggered, whether a password matches.

A char stores exactly one symbol. In Python, characters are written in single quotes: 'A', '9', '!'. A string is a sequence of characters — as long or short as needed, including an empty string "". In Python: name = "Priya".

When a user types a number using input(), Python receives it as a string by default. Trying to add two such strings gives concatenation, not arithmetic. For example: "5" + "3" gives "53", not 8. You must convert the input before doing any maths:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
year_of_birth = 2026 - age
print(year_of_birth)

Use int() for whole numbers and float() for decimals. This is one of the most common errors in exam answers — always check whether a variable storing user input has been converted to the right type.

Variables and Constants

A variable is a named location in memory whose value can change as the program executes. In Python, you create a variable simply by assigning a value to it: score = 0. Every variable has a name (its identifier), a value, and an implied data type.

A constant is a value that should stay fixed throughout the program. Python does not enforce constants with a keyword, but the convention is to write them in uppercase: MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3. Using a named constant makes maintenance far easier — if you later need to change the maximum to 5, you change it in one place rather than searching through every line of code for the number 3.

Key Fact

Meaningful identifier names make code readable and maintainable. livesRemaining is immediately clear; x or temp is not. Examiners award marks for meaningful identifiers when you write code — single-letter names (except conventional loop counters such as i) will cost marks.

Structured Data Types

Beyond the five primitives, Python supports structured types that group multiple values together. An array (implemented in Python as a list) holds an ordered sequence of values. A record groups related fields of potentially different types — implemented in Python using a dictionary. These are covered in detail in a later lesson.

Writing Readable Code

The specification requires you to write code that is easy for another programmer to read. Four techniques contribute to readability: meaningful identifier names (already covered), correct indentation, useful comments, and consistent use of white space.

In Python, indentation is not optional — it defines code blocks. All statements inside an if, for or function body must be indented by the same amount (usually four spaces). Inconsistent indentation causes an IndentationError.

Hard to read (poor names, no comments, no spacing):

x=int(input(""))
if x>=50:
    print("P")
else:
    print("F")

Easy to read (meaningful names, comment at block level, spacing):

# Check whether a student has passed their exam
score = int(input("Enter exam score: "))

if score >= 50:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")

Notice: the comment explains the purpose of the block, not what each individual line does. Over-commenting — adding a comment to every single line — makes code harder to read, not easier. A common mistake in exam answers is writing more comment text than code.

Initialisation and Assignment

Before you can use a variable, you must give it an initial value. This is called initialisation. For example, a score counter should start at zero: score = 0. Running total variables, list index counters and flag variables all need initialisation before a loop begins. Failing to initialise a variable causes a NameError in Python — the program tries to use a name it has never seen before.

When you encounter new code, try to predict its output before you run it. Consider:

total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total = total + i
print(total)

Predict: range(1, 5) produces 1, 2, 3, 4. The loop adds each to total, giving 1, 3, 6, 10. The output is 10. Then run it to verify. This predict-then-run habit is especially useful for tackling “Complete a Trace Table” questions in your exam.
exam_tip_html: For “Define” questions on data types, be precise: a char holds exactly one character; a string holds a sequence of characters. Examiners penalise vague answers such as “it holds text.” For “Identify” questions about which data type to use, pick the most specific type — if a value is always a whole number, choose integer rather than real. For “Write” questions, always use meaningful identifier names and add one block-level comment — not a comment on every line.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Python has five primitive data types: integer, real (float), Boolean, char and string. Use the term real in written exam answers.
  • Variables hold values that can change; constants (uppercase by convention) hold values that must not change. Both need meaningful identifier names.
  • Readable code uses meaningful identifiers, correct indentation, block-level comments (not per-line) and consistent white space.

practice_questions.text: State the most appropriate data type for storing a student's date of birth in the format DD/MM/YYYY.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: String (1). The format contains slashes and leading zeros — it cannot be stored as an integer or real without losing information.
Secure: Correct with minor explanation gap.
Developing: Character (a single symbol only — cannot hold the full date).
Emerging: Integer or Boolean.

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by a constant in a Python program. Give one reason why a programmer would use a constant rather than a variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A constant is a named value (1) that is set once and should not change during execution (1); reason — if the value needs updating, it is changed in one place rather than in every occurrence in the code (1); example given, e.g. TAX_RATE or MAX_LIVES (1).
Secure: Constant correctly defined with a weak reason.
Developing: One part (definition or reason) correct.
Emerging: Confuses constant with variable.

practice_questions.text:
A Python program contains the line:
score = input("Enter score: ")
total = score + 10
Explain why this will cause an error, and write a corrected version of the second line.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The input() function returns a string (1) so adding 10 (an integer) to a string is a type error (1); corrected line: total = int(score) + 10 (1); explanation that int() converts the string to an integer (1).
Secure: Error correctly identified with partial correction.
Developing: Identifies an error exists but misnames the type.
Emerging: No understanding of type conversion.

practice_questions.text: Identify the data type of each of the following Python values: (a) True  (b) 3.14  (c) 'K'  (d) 42
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) Boolean (1), (b) real/float (1), (c) char (1), (d) integer (1).
Secure: Three correct.
Developing: Two correct.
Emerging: One or none correct.

practice_questions.text:
Complete a trace table for the following Python code. Show the value of total after each iteration.
total = 0
for i in range(1, 4):
    total = total + i
print(total)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: i=1 total=1; i=2 total=3; i=3 total=6; output 6. One mark per correct row (3 rows + output).
Secure: Two rows correct plus correct final output.
Developing: One row correct.
Emerging: No understanding of loop accumulation.

practice_questions.text:
A programmer writes the following code:
MAX_SIZE = 100
studentnumber = 0
Write a brief explanation of why MAX_SIZE follows good programming practice, and suggest an improvement to the identifier name for the second variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: MAX_SIZE is in uppercase — conventional for constants (1); its name clearly describes its purpose (1); it can be changed in one place if the limit changes (1); studentnumber could be improved to student_number or studentNumber (1); a better name describes the purpose more precisely, e.g. currentStudentNumber or studentCount (1); explanation of why the improvement matters for readability and maintenance (1).
Secure: Three or four valid points with partial explanation.
Developing: One or two points without full reasoning.
Emerging: Vague or no understanding of naming conventions.

knowledge_checks.q: Which data type should be used to store the value True or False in Python?
A student types their age using input(). What data type does Python store this as by default?
A named value that is set once and must not change during program execution is called a _____.
In Python, a number with a decimal point has a data type called _____ (in exam answers, use the spec term 'real').
Match each Python value to its data type.

flashcard_questions.q: Which data type stores a number with a decimal point in Python?
flashcard_questions.a: Real (Python calls it float; use 'real' in exam answers).

flashcard_questions.q: What Python function converts a string input to a whole number?
What is the term for a named storage location whose value can change during program execution?
What convention signals that an identifier is a constant in Python?
flashcard_questions.a: Writing it in UPPERCASE, e.g. MAX_ATTEMPTS.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is MAX_SCORE better practice than the number 100 scattered through a program?
flashcard_questions.a: Changing the value in one place updates the whole program.

flashcard_questions.q: A char holds _____ character(s); a string holds _____.
flashcard_questions.a: One character / a sequence of zero or more characters.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the Python error raised when you reference a variable before assigning it a value.
What does over-commenting mean, and why is it a problem?
flashcard_questions.a: Adding a comment to every line — it clutters code and reduces readability.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'initialisation' mean for a variable?
flashcard_questions.a: Giving the variable its first value before it is used in the program.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two Python Boolean values? (Give exact syntax.)
flashcard_questions.a: True and False — capital first letter required.

flashcard_questions.q: Cloze: In Python, indentation is _____ — it defines code blocks and inconsistency causes an IndentationError.

glossary_terms.definition: A classification that tells Python what kind of data is being stored, how much memory to allocate, and what operations are valid on it.
A whole number with no decimal part, which can be positive, negative or zero.
A number that can include a decimal point; called float in Python but referred to as real in exam answers.
A data type that can hold only one of two values: True or False.
A data type that holds exactly one character, such as a letter, digit or punctuation mark.
A data type that holds a sequence of zero or more characters, used to store text such as names, messages and postcodes.
A named storage location in memory whose value can change while the program runs.
A named value that is set once and must not change during program execution; conventionally written in uppercase to signal that it should not be altered.
The name given to a variable, constant or subprogram in a program; should clearly describe its purpose.
A structured data type that stores an ordered collection of values of the same type, accessed by position using an index.
A structured data type that groups related fields of different types together under one named structure, such as a student record holding a name, age and score.
